claim: The PVH exhibited 306% higher c-fos expression during the active period (23:00) compared to the inactive period (11:00) in mice.
source: Immunohistochemistry results showed a 306 % higher number of c-fos-positive cells in the PVH from mice sacrificed in the active period (23:00) compared with those sacrificed in the inactive period (11:00) (Figure 1A and B)
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data presented in Figure 1A and B showing quantified c-fos expression differences between time points.

claim: More than 90% of the PVH consists of glutamatergic neurons expressing vesicle glutamate transporter 2 (vglut2).
source: More than 90 % of the PVH consists of glutamatergic neurons expressing vesicle glutamate transporter 2 (vglut2), whereas GABAergic neurons are more scarcely represented (Vong et al., 2011; Xu et al., 2013; Ziegler et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to three published studies (Vong et al., 2011; Xu et al., 2013; Ziegler et al., 2005).

claim: PVHvglut2 neurons receive direct inputs from the PVT and PB.
source: As shown in Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1, we found that PVHvglut2 neurons received direct inputs from many regions. Among them, the PVT and PB are considered as two important wake-promoting nuclei
evidence: The claim is supported by rabies virus-mediated monosynaptic retrograde tracing data shown in Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: PVHvglut2 neuronal activities during wakefulness were significantly higher than those during NREM sleep.
source: PVHvglut2 neuronal activities during wakefulness were significantly higher than those during NREM sleep (Figure 2C–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by fiber photometry data presented in Figure 2C-E showing calcium signal differences across vigilance states.

claim: PVH neurons exhibited a higher firing rate during wakefulness than during sleep.
source: PVH neurons exhibited a higher firing rate during wakefulness than during sleep (Figure 2G and H).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo multichannel electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 2G and H.

claim: At the onset of behavioral arousal from NREM sleep, the mean firing rate of PVH neurons increased from 4.83 Hz to 13.52 Hz.
source: At the onset of behavioral arousal from NREM sleep, the mean firing rate increased from 4.83 Hz to 13.52 Hz (Figure 2I).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data showing firing rate changes during state transitions presented in Figure 2I.

claim: Chemogenetic activation of PVHvglut2 neurons caused a potent increase in wakefulness lasting approximately 9 hours.
source: At the beginning of the light phase (zeitgeber time 2 [ZT2]; 9:00), chemogenetic activation of PVHvglut2 neurons caused a potent increase in wakefulness lasting approximately 9 hr and concomitantly decreased both NREM and REM sleep (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by polysomnographic recordings following CNO administration in hM3Dq-expressing mice shown in Figure 3C.

claim: CNO administration resulted in a 140.0% increase in total wakefulness during the 9 hr post-injection period.
source: CNO administration (3 mg/kg) resulted in a 140.0 % increase in total wakefulness, as well as 81.6% and 94.5% reduction in NREM and REM sleep, respectively, during the 9 hr post-injection period (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantified sleep-wake data following chemogenetic activation presented in Figure 3D.

claim: There was no sleep rebound following the long-lasting wakefulness induced by PVHvglut2 activation.
source: However, there was no sleep rebound followed the long-lasting wakefulness, as indicated by no change in the time spent in NREM sleep during the following dark period (19:00–07:00; Figure 3E).
evidence: The claim is supported by sleep data from the dark period following CNO-induced wakefulness shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Optical stimulation of PVHvglut2 neurons during NREM sleep reliably induced transitions to wakefulness in a frequency-dependent manner.
source: Optical stimulation of PVHvglut2 neurons during NREM sleep reliably induced transitions to wakefulness in a frequency-dependent manner (Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is supported by optogenetic stimulation experiments with varying frequencies shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Sustained activation of PVHvglut2 neurons via semi-chronic optical stimulation significantly increased the amount of wakefulness from 12.3 ± 1.8 min at baseline to 48.6 ± 1.5 min after stimulation.
source: Sustained activation of PVHvglut2 neurons via semi-chronic optical stimulation (10 ms blue-light pulses at 20 Hz for 25 s, every 60 s for 1 hr) significantly increased the amount of wakefulness in ChR2-mCherry mice compared with that of the baseline control between 09:00 and 10:00 (12.3 ± 1.8 min at baseline vs. 48.6 ± 1.5 min after stimulation, n = 5; Figure 4F).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantified wakefulness data during chronic optogenetic stimulation presented in Figure 4F.

claim: Optogenetic stimulation of ChR2-expressing PVH terminals evoked excitatory postsynaptic currents in most patch-recorded PB neurons (n = 6 cells).
source: Optogenetic stimulation (10 ms pulses at 10 Hz for 2 s) of the ChR2-expressing PVH terminals evoked excitatory postsynaptic currents (EPSCs) in most of the patch-recorded PB (n = 6 cells, Figure 5B)
evidence: The claim is supported by whole-cell patch-clamp recordings from PB neurons shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Optogenetic stimulation of ChR2-expressing PVH terminals evoked excitatory postsynaptic currents in most patch-recorded LSv neurons (n = 8 cells).
source: Optogenetic stimulation (10 ms pulses at 10 Hz for 2 s) of the ChR2-expressing PVH terminals evoked excitatory postsynaptic currents (EPSCs) in most of the patch-recorded PB (n = 6 cells, Figure 5B) or LSv (n = 8 cells, Figure 5F) neurons.
evidence: The claim is supported by whole-cell patch-clamp recordings from LSv neurons shown in Figure 5F.

claim: 20 Hz stimulation of the bilateral PB induced a transition from NREM sleep to wakefulness with a latency of 1.0 ± 0.8 s.
source: Moreover, 20 Hz stimulation of the bilateral PB or LSv induced a shorter transition from NREM sleep to wakefulness (latency for PB: 1.0 ± 0.8 s, latency for LSv: 1.2 ± 0.9 s) compared with that of the control (Figure 5C and G).
evidence: The claim is supported by optogenetic circuit manipulation data showing transition latencies presented in Figure 5C and G.

claim: 20 Hz stimulation of the bilateral LSv induced a transition from NREM sleep to wakefulness with a latency of 1.2 ± 0.9 s.
source: Moreover, 20 Hz stimulation of the bilateral PB or LSv induced a shorter transition from NREM sleep to wakefulness (latency for PB: 1.0 ± 0.8 s, latency for LSv: 1.2 ± 0.9 s) compared with that of the control (Figure 5C and G).
evidence: The claim is supported by optogenetic circuit manipulation data showing transition latencies presented in Figure 5C and G.

claim: Optogenetic activation of the PVHvglut2→NTS pathway did not alter sleep-wake states.
source: However, optogenetic activation of the other two pathways— PVHvglut2→NTS and PVHvglut2→PVT pathways did not alter sleep—wake states (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by optogenetic circuit manipulation data showing no effect on sleep-wake states presented in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Optogenetic activation of the PVHvglut2→PVT pathway did not alter sleep-wake states.
source: However, optogenetic activation of the other two pathways— PVHvglut2→NTS and PVHvglut2→PVT pathways did not alter sleep—wake states (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by optogenetic circuit manipulation data showing no effect on sleep-wake states presented in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Chemogenetic activation of PVHOT neurons induced a 49.4% increase in wakefulness that lasted for 1 hr.
source: We found that chemogenetic activation either PVHOT or PVHPDYN neurons both induced increased wakefulness (49.4% and 75.8%, respectively) and decreased NREM sleep (53.9% and 88.5%, respectively) that lasted for 1 hr (Figure 6C and F).
evidence: The claim is supported by polysomnographic recordings following CNO administration in OTCre mice expressing hM3Dq shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Chemogenetic activation of PVHPDYN neurons induced a 75.8% increase in wakefulness that lasted for 1 hr.
source: We found that chemogenetic activation either PVHOT or PVHPDYN neurons both induced increased wakefulness (49.4% and 75.8%, respectively) and decreased NREM sleep (53.9% and 88.5%, respectively) that lasted for 1 hr (Figure 6C and F).
evidence: The claim is supported by polysomnographic recordings following CNO administration in PDYNCre mice expressing hM3Dq shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Chemogenetic activation of PVHCRH neurons caused a potent increase in wakefulness lasting approximately 3 hr.
source: Similarly, chemogenetic activation of PVHCRH neurons caused a potent increase in wakefulness lasting approximately 3 hr and concomitantly decreased both NREM and REM sleep.
evidence: The claim is supported by polysomnographic recordings following CNO administration in CRHCre mice expressing hM3Dq.

claim: CNO administration in PVHCRH-hM3Dq mice induced a 75.8% increase in wakefulness during the 3 hr post-injection period.
source: CNO administration (3 mg/kg) induced a 75.8 % increase in wakefulness and a 67.7% and 46.3% reduction in NREM and REM sleep, respectively, during the 3 hr post-injection period (Figure 6I).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantified sleep-wake data following chemogenetic activation of PVHCRH neurons presented in Figure 6I.

claim: Chemogenetic inhibition of PVHvglut2 neurons resulted in a 64.0% increase in NREM sleep during the 5 hr post-injection period.
source: At the beginning of the dark phase (ZT14; 21:00), CNO injection resulted in a 64.0 % increase in NREM sleep during the 5 hr post-injection period, which was accompanied by a 26.0 % decrease in wakefulness (Figure 7C).
evidence: The claim is supported by polysomnographic recordings following CNO administration in hM4Di-expressing mice shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Ablation of PVHvglut2 neurons showed a 28.6% decrease in the amount of wakefulness during the dark period.
source: Compared with the control group, mice that underwent PVHvglut2 neuronal ablation showed a 28.6 % decrease in the amount of wakefulness and a 74.7 % increase in the amount of NREM sleep during the dark period.
evidence: The claim is supported by polysomnographic recordings in mice with PVHvglut2 neuronal ablation using AAV-taCasp3.

claim: Ablation of PVHvglut2 neurons induced a 20.8% reduction in wakefulness across an entire 24 hr light/dark cycle.
source: Similarly, ablation of PVHvglut2 neurons induced a 20.8 % reduction in wakefulness and 30.6 % increase in NREM sleep across an entire 24 hr light/dark cycle (Figure 7F).
evidence: The claim is supported by 24-hour polysomnographic recordings in mice with PVHvglut2 neuronal ablation shown in Figure 7F.

claim: Ablation of PVHvglut2 neurons induced a 30.6% increase in NREM sleep across an entire 24 hr light/dark cycle.
source: Similarly, ablation of PVHvglut2 neurons induced a 20.8 % reduction in wakefulness and 30.6 % increase in NREM sleep across an entire 24 hr light/dark cycle (Figure 7F).
evidence: The claim is supported by 24-hour polysomnographic recordings in mice with PVHvglut2 neuronal ablation shown in Figure 7F.

claim: Hypersomnolence disorder (HD) is characterized by excessive sleep.
source: Hypersomnolence disorder (HD) is characterized by excessive sleep, which is a common sequela following stroke, infection, or tumorigenesis.
evidence: The claim represents established clinical knowledge about the defining characteristic of HD.

claim: HD is a common sequela following stroke, infection, or tumorigenesis.
source: Hypersomnolence disorder (HD) is characterized by excessive sleep, which is a common sequela following stroke, infection, or tumorigenesis.
evidence: The claim represents established clinical knowledge about conditions associated with HD.

claim: Lesions of a single wake-promoting nucleus, or even two simultaneously, did not exert serious HD.
source: However, lesions of a single wake-promoting nucleus, or even two simultaneously, did not exert serious HD.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from prior research findings in the field.

claim: Von Economo first proposed a hypersomnia-controlling region located in the posterior hypothalamus from observations of marked somnolence in patients with epidemic encephalitis lethargic.
source: Von Economo first proposed a hypersomnia-controlling region located in the posterior hypothalamus from observations of marked somnolence in patients with epidemic encephalitis lethargic (Saper et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Saper et al., 2001.

claim: A brainstem ascending reticular activating system (ARAS) is responsible for wakefulness.
source: Furthermore, Moruzzi et al. and other studies have revealed that a brainstem ascending reticular activating system (ARAS) is responsible for wakefulness (Moruzzi and Magoun, 1949; Xu et al., 2015; Carter et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies (Moruzzi and Magoun, 1949; Xu et al., 2015; Carter et al., 2010).

claim: Cell-body-specific ablation or inhibition of LDT, BF, PPT cholinergic neurons, DRN serotonergic neurons, and LC noradrenergic neurons yields limited alterations in sleep.
source: However, cell-body-specific ablation or inhibition of components of the ARAS—including the laterodorsal tegmentum (LDT), basal forebrain (BF), pedunculopontine tegmental nucleus (PPT) cholinergic neurons, dorsal raphe nucleus (DRN) serotonergic neurons, and locus coeruleus (LC) noradrenergic neurons—yields limited alterations in sleep (Lu et al., 2006b; Chen et al., 2016; Fuller et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies (Lu et al., 2006b; Chen et al., 2016; Fuller et al., 2011).

claim: Dysfunction of orexinergic neurons in the LH results in narcolepsy and sleep fragmentation.
source: Dysfunction of orexinergic neurons in the LH results in narcolepsy and sleep fragmentation (Lu et al., 2006b; Chemelli et al., 1999; Gerashchenko et al., 2003; Adamantidis et al., 2007)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies (Lu et al., 2006b; Chemelli et al., 1999; Gerashchenko et al., 2003; Adamantidis et al., 2007).

claim: PB glutamatergic neurons play a role in triggering hypercapnia-induced arousal in obstructive sleep apnea (OSA).
source: PB glutamatergic neurons are considered to serve as a hub, as they receive afferent chemosensory information and play a role in triggering hypercapnia-induced arousal in obstructive sleep apnea (OSA), whereas ablation of PB glutamatergic neurons decreases hypercapnia-induced arousal (Guyenet and Bayliss, 2015; Yokota et al., 2015; Kaur et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies (Guyenet and Bayliss, 2015; Yokota et al., 2015; Kaur et al., 2013).

claim: Ablation of LH orexinergic neurons and the lateral PB have little effect on sleep under baseline conditions.
source: The further amazing research found that ablation of LH orexinergic neurons and the lateral PB (LPB) have little effect on sleep under baseline conditions, and deletion of the medial PB (MPB) causes only a modest (approximately 20%) reduction in wakefulness (Fuller et al., 2011; Gerashchenko et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to two studies (Fuller et al., 2011; Gerashchenko et al., 2003).

claim: Deletion of the medial PB (MPB) causes only a modest (approximately 20%) reduction in wakefulness.
source: The further amazing research found that ablation of LH orexinergic neurons and the lateral PB (LPB) have little effect on sleep under baseline conditions, and deletion of the medial PB (MPB) causes only a modest (approximately 20%) reduction in wakefulness (Fuller et al., 2011; Gerashchenko et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to two studies (Fuller et al., 2011; Gerashchenko et al., 2003).

claim: Patients with Parkinson's disease (PD), Alzheimer's disease (AD), Kleine-Levin Syndrome, and idiopathic hypersomnia (IH) show hypersomnolence.
source: Clinically, patients with Parkinson's disease (PD), Alzheimer's disease (AD), Kleine-Levin Syndrome, and idiopathic hypersomnia (IH), in which LH orexinergic and PB glutamatergic neurons are thought to function normally, still show hypersomnolence (Bollu et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Bollu et al., 2018.

claim: The PVH is located in the ventral diencephalon adjacent to the third ventricle.
source: The PVH is located in the ventral diencephalon adjacent to the third ventricle (Qin et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Qin et al., 2018.

claim: PVHvglut2 neurons co-express corticotropin-releasing hormone (CRH).
source: PVHvglut2 neurons co-express corticotropin-releasing hormone (CRH) (Zhang et al., 2020), oxytocin (OT) (Hung et al., 2017), and prodynorphin (PDYN) (Li et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Zhang et al., 2020.

claim: PVHvglut2 neurons co-express oxytocin (OT).
source: PVHvglut2 neurons co-express corticotropin-releasing hormone (CRH) (Zhang et al., 2020), oxytocin (OT) (Hung et al., 2017), and prodynorphin (PDYN) (Li et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Hung et al., 2017.

claim: PVHvglut2 neurons co-express prodynorphin (PDYN).
source: PVHvglut2 neurons co-express corticotropin-releasing hormone (CRH) (Zhang et al., 2020), oxytocin (OT) (Hung et al., 2017), and prodynorphin (PDYN) (Li et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Li et al., 2019.

claim: The PVT and PB exhibit higher activities during wakefulness than during sleep.
source: Among them, the PVT and PB are considered as two important wake-promoting nuclei; they exhibit higher activities during wakefulness than during sleep, and their activation induces rapid transitions from sleep to wakefulness (Ren et al., 2018; Qiu et al., 2016; Xu et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies (Ren et al., 2018; Qiu et al., 2016; Xu et al., 2021).

claim: Activation of the PVT and PB induces rapid transitions from sleep to wakefulness.
source: Among them, the PVT and PB are considered as two important wake-promoting nuclei; they exhibit higher activities during wakefulness than during sleep, and their activation induces rapid transitions from sleep to wakefulness (Ren et al., 2018; Qiu et al., 2016; Xu et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies (Ren et al., 2018; Qiu et al., 2016; Xu et al., 2021).

claim: Chemogenetic activation of PVHvglut2 neurons significantly increased EEG low delta power (0.25–1.00 Hz) and decreased high delta power (1.25–4.75 Hz).
source: Compared with vehicle injection, chemogenetic activation of PVHvglut2 neurons significantly increased EEG low delta power (0.25–1.00 Hz) and decreased high delta power (1.25–4.75 Hz) (Figure 3F).
evidence: The claim is supported by EEG power density analysis data presented in Figure 3F.

claim: Chemogenetic activation of PVHvglut2 neurons induced an increase in heart rate and temperature for 3 hr.
source: We found that chemogenetic activation of PVHvglut2 neurons induced an increase in heart rate and temperature for 3 hr, both of which peaked at about 2 hr after injection and returned to the baseline level at about 3 hr following administration of CNO.
evidence: The claim is supported by telemetry measurements of heart rate and temperature following CNO administration.

claim: Chemogenetic activation of PVHvglut2 neurons significantly increased the CRH level at 2, 3, and 4 hr after injection.
source: As shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2C, chemogenetic activation of PVHvglut2 neurons significantly increased the CRH level at 2, 3, and 4 hr after injection, while the CORT level of the CNO group was only higher than that of the vehicle group at 3 hr following CNO administration.
evidence: The claim is supported by ELISA measurements of serum CRH levels shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2C.

claim: The CORT level of the CNO group was only higher than that of the vehicle group at 3 hr following CNO administration in PVHvglut2-hM3Dq mice.
source: As shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2C, chemogenetic activation of PVHvglut2 neurons significantly increased the CRH level at 2, 3, and 4 hr after injection, while the CORT level of the CNO group was only higher than that of the vehicle group at 3 hr following CNO administration.
evidence: The claim is supported by ELISA measurements of serum CORT levels shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2C.

claim: PVHvglut2 neurons send widespread projections to distinct brain structures.
source: As our results show, PVHvglut2 neurons send widespread projections to distinct brain structures.
evidence: The claim is based on anterograde tracing data showing multiple projection targets.

claim: PVHCRH, PVHOT, and PVHPDYN neurons all project to the median eminence area (ME).
source: According to previous research, PVHCRH, PVHOT, and PVHPDYN neurons all project to the median eminence area (ME) (Xu et al., 2019; Li et al., 2019), which serves as an interface between the neural and peripheral endocrine systems.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to two studies (Xu et al., 2019; Li et al., 2019).

claim: The PVH→LSv projection exhibited scalable control over feeding and negative emotional states.
source: Previous studies reported that the PVH→LSv projection exhibited scalable control over feeding and negative emotional states (Xu et al., 2019)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Xu et al., 2019.

claim: PVHPDYN→PB projections are necessary for satiety.
source: and PVHPDYN→PB projections are necessary for satiety (Li et al., 2019), which are all wakefulness-required behaviors.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Li et al., 2019.

claim: A robust reduction in the number of PVH neurons has been found in MDD, BD, AD, and PD patients.
source: A robust reduction in the number of PVH neurons has been found in MDD, BD, AD, and PD patients (Manaye et al., 2005; Baloyannis et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to three studies (Manaye et al., 2005; Baloyannis et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2017).

claim: Lesions of the PPT and the ventral sublaterodorsal nucleus (vSLD) result in a 20–30% reduction in baseline wakefulness.
source: Lu et al have reported that lesions of the PPT and the ventral sublaterodorsal nucleus (vSLD) result in a 20–30% reduction in baseline wakefulness (Lu et al., 2006b).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Lu et al., 2006b.

claim: Bidirectional chemogenetic manipulations that inhibit the PPT or activate SLD neurons have little influence on baseline sleep.
source: However, bidirectional chemogenetic manipulations that inhibit the PPT or activate SLD neurons have been shown to have little influence on baseline sleep (Kroeger et al., 2017; Erickson et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to two studies (Kroeger et al., 2017; Erickson et al., 2019).

claim: Chemogenetic activation of wake-promoting neuronal populations does not enhance the homeostatic drive for sleep.
source: This finding is in accordance with previous studies using chemogenetics to specifically activate wake-promoting neuronal populations (Pedersen et al., 2017; Erickson et al., 2019; Anaclet et al., 2015; Venner et al., 2016) and indicates that chemogenetic activation of wake-promoting neuronal populations does not enhance the homeostatic drive for sleep.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies (Pedersen et al., 2017; Erickson et al., 2019; Anaclet et al., 2015; Venner et al., 2016) and inference from the current findings.

claim: The PVH is estimated to consist of approximately 56,000 neurons in humans.
source: The PVH is estimated to consist of approximately 56,000 neurons in humans (Morton, 1969), of which 25,000 neurons express OT (Wierda et al., 1991), 21,000 neurons express PDYN (Li et al., 2019; Purba et al., 1993; Purba et al., 1995) and 2000 neurons express CRH (Xu et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Morton, 1969.

claim: 25,000 neurons in the human PVH express OT.
source: The PVH is estimated to consist of approximately 56,000 neurons in humans (Morton, 1969), of which 25,000 neurons express OT (Wierda et al., 1991), 21,000 neurons express PDYN (Li et al., 2019; Purba et al., 1993; Purba et al., 1995) and 2000 neurons express CRH (Xu et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Wierda et al., 1991.

claim: 21,000 neurons in the human PVH express PDYN.
source: The PVH is estimated to consist of approximately 56,000 neurons in humans (Morton, 1969), of which 25,000 neurons express OT (Wierda et al., 1991), 21,000 neurons express PDYN (Li et al., 2019; Purba et al., 1993; Purba et al., 1995) and 2000 neurons express CRH (Xu et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to three studies (Li et al., 2019; Purba et al., 1993; Purba et al., 1995).

claim: 2000 neurons in the human PVH express CRH.
source: The PVH is estimated to consist of approximately 56,000 neurons in humans (Morton, 1969), of which 25,000 neurons express OT (Wierda et al., 1991), 21,000 neurons express PDYN (Li et al., 2019; Purba et al., 1993; Purba et al., 1995) and 2000 neurons express CRH (Xu et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Xu et al., 2020.

claim: Almost 100% of neurons expressing CRH, PDYN and OXT were found to co-express with vglut2 in the middle PVH and posterior PVH.
source: Almost 100 % of neurons expressing CRH, PDYN and OXT were found to co-express with vglut2 in the middle PVH and posterior PVH, which were also the main distribution regions of these three neuropeptides populations in the PVH (Ziegler et al., 2005; Holmes et al., 1986).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to two studies (Ziegler et al., 2005; Holmes et al., 1986).

claim: PVHCRH neurons regulate stress, fear, and the immune response, as well as neuroendocrine and autonomic functions.
source: PVHCRH neurons regulate stress, fear, and the immune response, as well as neuroendocrine and autonomic functions (Zhang et al., 2020; Xu et al., 2019; Kondoh et al., 2016; Mezey et al., 1984; Winter and Jurek, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies (Zhang et al., 2020; Xu et al., 2019; Kondoh et al., 2016; Mezey et al., 1984; Winter and Jurek, 2019).

claim: Exposure to various stressors induces CRH and OT release into the peripheral circulation.
source: There is mounting evidence that exposure to various stressors induces CRH and OT release into the peripheral circulation (Yuan et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Yuan et al., 2019.

claim: CRH serves as the starting point and main driver of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis.
source: CRH serves as the starting point and main driver of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis (Zhang et al., 2020; Füzesi et al., 2016; Windle et al., 2004), while OT inhibits the activity of the HPA axis (Daviu et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to three studies (Zhang et al., 2020; Füzesi et al., 2016; Windle et al., 2004).

claim: OT inhibits the activity of the HPA axis.
source: CRH serves as the starting point and main driver of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis (Zhang et al., 2020; Füzesi et al., 2016; Windle et al., 2004), while OT inhibits the activity of the HPA axis (Daviu et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Daviu et al., 2020.

claim: PVHCRH neurons orchestrate stress-related behaviors, such as grooming, fear, rearing, and walking.
source: PVHCRH neurons orchestrate stress-related behaviors, such as grooming, fear, rearing, and walking (Windle et al., 2004; Xiao et al., 2017)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to two studies (Windle et al., 2004; Xiao et al., 2017).

claim: PVHOT neurons modulate reward circuits and play a role in mitigating the stress response.
source: while PVHOT neurons modulate reward circuits and play a role in mitigating the stress response (Yuan et al., 2019; Ono et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to two studies (Yuan et al., 2019; Ono et al., 2020).

claim: PVHCRH neurons play a role in the circadian regulation of wakefulness.
source: Considering that PVHCRH neurons play a role in the circadian regulation of wakefulness (Li et al., 2020a)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Li et al., 2020a.

claim: Optogenetic stimulation of PVHCRH neurons can simulate stress-induced insomnia.
source: and optogenetic stimulation of PVHCRH neurons can simulate stress-induced insomnia (Spencer and Deak, 2017)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Spencer and Deak, 2017.

claim: PVHPDYN neurons are key regulators of satiety.
source: PVHPDYN neurons are key regulators of satiety, and they project to the PB (Li et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Li et al., 2019.

claim: Chemogenetic activation of the PB produced ~11 hr of continuous wakefulness in rats.
source: Furthermore, the PVH sends direct projections to the PB, and it was reported that chemogenetic activation of the PB produced ~11 hr of continuous wakefulness in rats (Qiu et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Qiu et al., 2016.

claim: Glucocorticoid hormones (CORT for mice) are the effector hormones of the HPA axis neuroendocrine system.
source: Glucocorticoid hormones (CORT for mice) are the effector hormones of the HPA axis neuroendocrine system, which are regulated by CRH (secreted by neurons in the medial parvocellular portion of the PVH) and produce direct negative feedback inhibition of CRH neurons in the PVH (Purba et al., 1994).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Purba et al., 1994 and represents established knowledge about the HPA axis.

claim: Glucocorticoid hormones produce direct negative feedback inhibition of CRH neurons in the PVH.
source: Glucocorticoid hormones (CORT for mice) are the effector hormones of the HPA axis neuroendocrine system, which are regulated by CRH (secreted by neurons in the medial parvocellular portion of the PVH) and produce direct negative feedback inhibition of CRH neurons in the PVH (Purba et al., 1994).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Purba et al., 1994.

claim: HD is one of the most common symptoms in many neurological disorders and mental diseases, including PD, AD, IH, OSA, Huntington's disease, major depressive disorder (MDD), bipolar disorder (BD), Kleine-Levin syndrome, and depression.
source: HD is one of the most common symptoms in many neurological disorders and mental diseases, including PD, AD, IH, OSA, Huntington's disease, major depressive disorder (MDD), bipolar disorder (BD), Kleine-Levin syndrome, and depression (Mahowald and Schenck, 2005; Bollu et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to two studies (Mahowald and Schenck, 2005; Bollu et al., 2018).

claim: PVHvglut2 neurons were most active during wakefulness.
source: By using vesicular glutamate transporter 2 (vglut2Cre) mice together with fiber photometry, multichannel electrophysiological recordings, and genetic approaches, we found that PVHvglut2 neurons were most active during wakefulness.
evidence: The claim is supported by fiber photometry and electrophysiological data showing state-dependent activity patterns.

claim: Chemogenetic activation of PVHvglut2 neurons induced wakefulness for 9 hr.
source: Chemogenetic activation of PVHvglut2 neurons induced wakefulness for 9 hr
evidence: The claim is supported by polysomnographic recordings following CNO administration in hM3Dq-expressing mice.

claim: Photostimulation of PVHvglut2→parabrachial complex circuits immediately drove transitions from sleep to wakefulness.
source: and photostimulation of PVHvglut2→parabrachial complex/ventral lateral septum circuits immediately drove transitions from sleep to wakefulness.
evidence: The claim is supported by optogenetic circuit manipulation experiments showing rapid sleep-to-wake transitions.

claim: Photostimulation of PVHvglut2→ventral lateral septum circuits immediately drove transitions from sleep to wakefulness.
source: and photostimulation of PVHvglut2→parabrachial complex/ventral lateral septum circuits immediately drove transitions from sleep to wakefulness.
evidence: The claim is supported by optogenetic circuit manipulation experiments showing rapid sleep-to-wake transitions.

claim: Lesioning of PVHvglut2 neurons dramatically decreased wakefulness.
source: Moreover, lesioning or chemogenetic inhibition of PVHvglut2 neurons dramatically decreased wakefulness.
evidence: The claim is supported by polysomnographic recordings in mice with PVHvglut2 neuronal ablation.

claim: Chemogenetic inhibition of PVHvglut2 neurons dramatically decreased wakefulness.
source: Moreover, lesioning or chemogenetic inhibition of PVHvglut2 neurons dramatically decreased wakefulness.
evidence: The claim is supported by polysomnographic recordings following CNO administration in hM4Di-expressing mice.

claim: The PVH is critical for arousal promotion and maintenance.
source: These results indicate that the PVH is critical for arousal promotion and maintenance.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the collective experimental findings showing bidirectional control of wakefulness by PVH neurons.

claim: HD is characterized by an irresistible need for sleep and an inability to stay awake during major waking episodes.
source: Hypersomnolence disorder (HD) is characterized by an irresistible need for sleep and an inability to stay awake during major waking episodes, which results in reduced function and overall worse life quality, highlighting its public health importance (Mahowald and Schenck, 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Mahowald and Schenck, 2005 and represents established clinical knowledge.

claim: Few dysfunctional wake-promoting nuclei have been identified to induce hypersomnia.
source: However, few dysfunctional wake-promoting nuclei have been identified to induce hypersomnia.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the literature review presented in the introduction.

claim: More than 16 wake-promoting nuclei have been identified in the last 100 years.
source: In the last 100 years, more than 16 wake-promoting nuclei have been identified.
evidence: The claim represents established knowledge from the field of sleep neuroscience.

claim: The LH, PB, TMN, PVT, VTA, and SUM have been demonstrated to be involved in arousal regulation.
source: Additionally, the lateral hypothalamic area (LH), parabrachial nucleus (PB), tuberomammilary nucleus (TMN), paraventricular nucleus of the thalamus (PVT), ventral tegmental area (VTA), and supramammillary nucleus (SUM) have also been demonstrated to be involved in arousal regulation (Lu et al., 2006b; Pedersen et al., 2017; Ren et al., 2018; Eban-Rothschild et al., 2016; Chemelli et al., 1999; Sherin et al., 1996).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies (Lu et al., 2006b; Pedersen et al., 2017; Ren et al., 2018; Eban-Rothschild et al., 2016; Chemelli et al., 1999; Sherin et al., 1996).

claim: Only LH orexinergic and PB glutamatergic neurons have been shown to be related to hypersomnia among wake-promoting nuclei.
source: However, among these wake-promoting nuclei, only LH orexinergic and PB glutamatergic neurons have been shown to be related to hypersomnia.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the literature review and represents a synthesis of prior research findings.

claim: A 15% reduction in baseline wakefulness is considered significant in previous studies.
source: In previous studies, a 15 % reduction in baseline wakefulness is considered significant (Lu et al., 2006b; Lu et al., 2006a).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to two studies (Lu et al., 2006b; Lu et al., 2006a).

claim: Bidirectional chemogenetic manipulations that inhibit the PPT have little influence on baseline sleep.
source: However, bidirectional chemogenetic manipulations that inhibit the PPT or activate SLD neurons have been shown to have little influence on baseline sleep (Kroeger et al., 2017; Erickson et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to two studies (Kroeger et al., 2017; Erickson et al., 2019).

claim: Activation of SLD neurons has little influence on baseline sleep.
source: However, bidirectional chemogenetic manipulations that inhibit the PPT or activate SLD neurons have been shown to have little influence on baseline sleep (Kroeger et al., 2017; Erickson et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to two studies (Kroeger et al., 2017; Erickson et al., 2019).

claim: Dysfunction of the PVH is crucial for the pathogenesis underlying HD.
source: In conclusion, our results indicate that dysfunction of the PVH is crucial for the pathogenesis underlying HD
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the collective experimental findings showing that PVH dysfunction causes hypersomnia-like behaviors.

claim: PVHvglut2 and their subtype neurons (PVHOT, PVHPDYN, and PVHCRH) are critical for wakefulness.
source: and PVHvglut2 and their subtype neurons (PVHOT, PVHPDYN, and PVHCRH) are critical for wakefulness.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the collective experimental findings showing that activation of these neuronal subtypes promotes wakefulness.

claim: Dysfunction of PVHPDYN neurons may represent one of the causes of sleep-related eating disorders.
source: We found that chemogenetic activation of PVHPDYN neurons induced short-duration wakefulness; hence, dysfunction of PVHPDYN neurons may represent one of the causes of sleep-related eating disorders .
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on the finding that PVHPDYN neurons regulate both satiety and wakefulness.

claim: The wake-promoting neural circuits of PVHvglut2 neurons played a more important role than endocrine and autonomic function changes in the 9 hr of wakefulness.
source: These results suggested that changes in glucocorticoid levels indeed occurred but did not last for 9 hr, so the long-lasting effects of wakefulness induced by PVH glutaminergic neurons' activation could only partly be explained by endocrine and autonomic function changes; the wake-promoting neural circuits of PVHvglut2 neurons played a more important role in the 9 hr of wakefulness.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the temporal mismatch between hormone levels and wakefulness duration.

claim: Dysfunction of the PVH may contribute to the occurrence of hypersomnia in MDD, BD, AD, and PD.
source: A robust reduction in the number of PVH neurons has been found in MDD, BD, AD, and PD patients (Manaye et al., 2005; Baloyannis et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2017). Thus, our present findings provide evidence that dysfunction of the PVH may contribute to the occurrence of hypersomnia in these diseases.
evidence: The claim is an inference connecting the current findings about PVH function with clinical observations of PVH neuron loss in these diseases.

claim: The PVH may represent one of the key arousal-controlling centers.
source: Therefore, we speculated that the PVH, in which most neurons are glutamatergic, may represent one of the key arousal-controlling centers.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on the observation of higher c-fos expression during the active period.

claim: PVHvglut2 neurons might act as a crucial node for the control of wakefulness.
source: Therefore, we speculated that PVHvglut2 neurons might act as a crucial node for the control of wakefulness.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on the finding that PVHvglut2 neurons receive inputs from wake-promoting nuclei PVT and PB.

claim: The neuronal firing rate in the PVH gradually decreased before sleep onset.
source: The neuronal firing rate in the PVH gradually decreased before sleep onset and increased during transitions from sleep to wakefulness (Figure 2I–K).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings showing firing rate changes during state transitions presented in Figure 2I-K.

claim: The neuronal firing rate in the PVH increased during transitions from sleep to wakefulness.
source: The neuronal firing rate in the PVH gradually decreased before sleep onset and increased during transitions from sleep to wakefulness (Figure 2I–K).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings showing firing rate changes during state transitions presented in Figure 2I-K.

claim: Optogenetic activation of PVHvglut2 neurons potently enhanced both the initiation and maintenance of wakefulness.
source: These findings demonstrate that optogenetic activation of PVHvglut2 neurons potently enhanced both the initiation and maintenance of wakefulness.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the optogenetic experiments showing both acute and chronic effects on wakefulness.

claim: PVHvglut2→PB and PVHvglut2→LSv circuits mediated the wakefulness-controlling effect of PVHvglut2 neurons.
source: These results demonstrated that PVHvglut2→PB and PVHvglut2→LSv circuits mediated the wakefulness-controlling effect of PVHvglut2 neurons.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the optogenetic circuit manipulation experiments showing that these pathways drive wakefulness.

claim: PVHvglut2 neurons are necessary for wakefulness regulation under physiological conditions.
source: These results indicate that PVHvglut2 neurons are necessary for wakefulness regulation under physiological conditions, and that dysfunction of these neurons may induce hypersomnia.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the loss-of-function experiments showing decreased wakefulness after ablation or inhibition.

claim: Dysfunction of PVHvglut2 neurons may induce hypersomnia.
source: These results indicate that PVHvglut2 neurons are necessary for wakefulness regulation under physiological conditions, and that dysfunction of these neurons may induce hypersomnia.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the loss-of-function experiments showing hypersomnia-like behaviors after ablation or inhibition.
